writingCoach.footer: These are guidelines, not rules: your adventure, your choices. Need concrete ideas? "Flesh out with AI" suggests options you accept one by one.

description.title: Short description
description.purpose: Reminds you, in one sentence, what is at play here when you prep the session or need to improvise.
questions: If you had to sum up this scene for another GM in ten seconds, what would you say?
What changes between the start and the end of the scene?
What do the characters come here looking for?
description.example: The PCs must convince the ferrywoman to take them across the river before dawn, even though she has already been paid to turn them in.
description.pitfall: Describing the set instead of the situation: "a tavern" says nothing about what is at play. A good description holds a goal or a tension.

nodeType.title: Node type
nodeType.purpose: Tells you, and the tool, what kind of scene this is: a location to explore, an encounter, an NPC, an event or a revelation.
questions: What will the players mostly do here: explore, fight, talk, endure or discover?
Does this scene deliver key information for what comes next? (then it's a revelation)
nodeType.example: An interrogation in the watch-house cellar is an "NPC" scene; finding the forged ledger hidden there is a "revelation".
nodeType.pitfall: Leaving everything as "generic": you lose sight of your adventure's pacing (three fights in a row then go unnoticed).

setting.title: Location and time
setting.purpose: Anchors the scene in a specific place and moment, so players can picture themselves there.
questions: Why this place and not another? What opportunities or obstacles does it offer?
Does the timing add a constraint: night, a crowd, a storm, a bell about to ring?
What can be used here: a staircase, a chandelier, a crowd to hide in?
setting.example: The fish market, an hour before opening: the stalls are empty, but the merchants arrive soon and word will spread.
setting.pitfall: A neutral place that brings nothing. A good location gives the players ideas and the GM complications.

atmosphere.title: Mood and atmosphere
atmosphere.purpose: Gives you sensory details to pick from during play, bringing the scene to life without over-preparing.
questions: What can be heard? Smelled? How warm or cold is it?
Which detail would a player remember after the session?
What emotion do you want to trigger: unease, wonder, urgency?
atmosphere.example: Smell of warm wax and stale incense. A steady drip somewhere in the dark. The cold of the stone seeps through the boots.
atmosphere.pitfall: Only describing what can be seen. Two senses other than sight do more than a long descriptive paragraph.

narration.title: Narration for players
narration.purpose: The text you read aloud to open the scene. It sets the stage and puts the players in a position to act.
questions: Can it be read in under a minute?
Does it end on a situation that calls for a reaction?
What must the players know, and what can they discover by asking questions?
narration.example: The mill door bangs in the wind. Inside, the millstone still turns, grinding nothing. On the floury floor, footprints lead to the trapdoor… and none come back. What do you do?
narration.pitfall: Deciding for the characters ("you are scared", "you step in carefully") or revealing everything at once. Describe what they perceive; let them choose what they feel and do.

gmNotes.title: GM notes and secrets
gmNotes.purpose: What the players don't know: hidden truths, NPC motives, what happens behind the scenes.
questions: What happens if the players do nothing?
What is the scene's main NPC hiding, and why?
Which piece of information must you be able to find in three seconds during play?
gmNotes.example:
• The ferrywoman was paid by the watch.
• Offered more, she hesitates, then betrays the watch.
• If the PCs dawdle: the patrol arrives at the third bell.
gmNotes.pitfall: Writing the whole scene as prose: in play, you won't find the information. Prefer short bullet points.

choices.title: Choices and consequences
choices.purpose: What gives players agency: their decisions truly change what happens next.
questions: What are at least two ways to approach the scene?
What does each option cost, or put at risk?
What happens on a failure? Does the scene still move forward?
choices.example: Bribe the ferrywoman: quick, but she will sell them out later. Threaten her: she gives in, but secretly warns the watch. Swim across: discreet, but the gear is lost or damaged.
choices.pitfall: "Fake choices": every option leads to the same result. And forgetting failure: a bad roll shouldn't stop the game, it should complicate it.

branches.title: Story branches
branches.purpose: Link the scene to the next ones based on what the players do, so no choice leads to a dead end.
questions: Where do the players go if they succeed? And if they fail?
What if they do something unexpected: flee, side with the enemy, ignore the lead?
Is a key piece of information reachable through a single path only?
branches.example: Success → "The smugglers' passage". Failure → "Arrested by the watch" (which also leads to the passage, but in chains). The ferrywoman's betrayal → "Ambush on the riverbank".
branches.pitfall: A single exit that depends on one successful roll. If the dice turn, the game stops: always keep a path open, even a costlier one.

combat.title: Combat or encounter
combat.purpose: Prepare an encounter that is easy to read, and interesting beyond trading blows.
questions: Why are these enemies fighting? What do they really want: flee, protect, steal, buy time?
Does the terrain change anything: high ground, water, darkness, things to knock over?
Can this fight be avoided, won another way, or lost without dying?
combat.example: Three smugglers aren't trying to kill anyone: they want to sink the boat holding the evidence. If they succeed, the fight is lost, even with every PC still standing.
combat.pitfall: The "bag of hit points" fight: with no goal other than taking the enemy down, it quickly becomes repetitive. Give each side a purpose.

purpose.title: Purpose of the scene
purpose.purpose: Every scene should bring something to the story. Knowing what you'd lose by cutting it helps decide what to keep, what to shorten, and what to improvise.
questions: What do the players learn here that they won't learn anywhere else?
What decision do they make, or what emotion do they feel?
If time runs short, can it be summed up in two sentences?
purpose.example: Without the inn, the players never meet Maëlis: they lose their only ally and the first lead to the tower.
purpose.pitfall: A scene that only exists to look nice or fill a session: players feel it, and the pacing collapses.

tactics.title: Enemy tactics and morale
tactics.purpose: Enemies who want to survive make a fight come alive: they use the terrain, protect their leader and know when to run. The GM then knows how to play them without improvising at random.
questions: How does the terrain favour them?
What makes them flee, surrender or negotiate?
Who do they protect, and what do they do if their leader falls?
tactics.example: The smugglers shoot from the boats and cut the moorings if approached. If the sergeant falls, they drop their weapons and offer to talk.
tactics.pitfall: Enemies who all fight to the death: the fight becomes plain hit point subtraction, with no choices for the players.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.purpose: Your overview: the starting situation, what happens, and how it might end.
questions: How are the characters involved?
What pushes them to act now rather than later?
What are two or three possible outcomes?
synopsis.example: The Vaulx bridge collapsed overnight and the village is cut off from the market. The bailiff blames the miners; the miners blame the bailiff. The PCs, stuck on the wrong bank, are the only ones nobody suspects.
synopsis.pitfall: Telling the story like a novel, including what the characters will do. Describe the situation and the forces at play, not the players' path.

objectives.title: Player objectives
objectives.purpose: What the characters are trying to achieve, from their own point of view.
questions: Do the players clearly know what they have to do?
How and when will they find out?
Can the objective shift along the way, after a revelation?
objectives.example: Find out who sabotaged the bridge, and prove it before the spring fair.
objectives.pitfall: An objective only the GM knows: the players wander without knowing what to do. If they can't put it into words, they don't have it.

stakes.title: Narrative stakes
stakes.purpose: What is at stake: what can be gained and, above all, what can be lost.
questions: What happens if the characters fail? Who suffers?
Does it affect a character personally?
Can the players lose something even when they succeed?
stakes.example: If the culprit isn't found, the bailiff will hang the brother of the blacksmith, the PCs' ally, as an example.
stakes.pitfall: Abstract stakes ("save the kingdom") with no face. An NPC the players like, in danger, matters more than an entire kingdom.

synopsis.title: Arc synopsis
synopsis.purpose: The arc's main thread: the central problem and what drives it forward.
questions: What is the central problem of this arc?
Who is responsible for it, and what do they want?
What happens if the characters don't step in?
synopsis.example: A guild of cartographers is slowly erasing villages from the official maps, to sell the "empty" land to the crown. Unchecked, three villages will vanish by winter.
synopsis.pitfall: A synopsis with no antagonist or opposing force: nothing drives the story, and the players wait for something to happen.

themes.title: Themes
themes.purpose: The story's colour, what it is really about beyond the plot.
questions: What moral question will the players face?
What hard choice will the arc force on them?
themes.example: Official truth versus lived truth. How far should one obey an unjust law?
themes.pitfall: Listing genres ("horror, mystery") instead of themes. A genre says how the story is told; a theme says what it is about.

stakes.title: Stakes
stakes.purpose: What changes, for the world and for the characters, depending on how the arc ends.
questions: What becomes of the world if the antagonist wins?
What do the characters gain by getting involved?
What do they personally risk?
stakes.example: If the guild wins, entire families lose their land, including one PC's home village.
stakes.pitfall: Stakes that don't concern the characters. Always tie the world's problem to something they care about.

rewards.title: Rewards and progression
rewards.purpose: What motivates the characters and marks their progress.
questions: Beyond gold, what can they gain: allies, reputation, knowledge, a place of their own?
How does the world react to their success?
rewards.example: The gratitude of the saved villages (a safe haven), a true map nobody else owns, and a sworn enemy within the guild.
rewards.pitfall: Only planning gold and items. The most memorable rewards change the characters' place in the world.

resolution.title: Planned resolution
resolution.purpose: The arc's possible endings, not a fixed one.
questions: What are two or three possible outcomes?
What happens if the characters fail?
What stays open for what comes next?
resolution.example: The guild is publicly exposed; or the PCs buy it out themselves; or the villages are lost and the next arc opens with the exodus.
resolution.pitfall: A single ending written in advance: the players' choices no longer matter. Prepare outcomes, not a script.

hiddenTruth.title: Hidden truth
hiddenTruth.purpose: The truth the players will piece together. Everything else follows from it: every clue, every revelation is a trace it left behind.
questions: What really happened, and who is responsible?
What traces did it leave, and where?
Can the players fully understand it by the end?
hiddenTruth.example: The regent poisoned the old king to rule in the prince's place. The court physician knows and keeps quiet out of fear.
hiddenTruth.pitfall: A truth too complicated to discover in play. If a player can't sum it up in one sentence at the end, simplify it.

hooks.title: Hooks
hooks.purpose: The reasons that push the characters to get involved. Several hooks of different kinds let players choose their motivation instead of having it imposed.
questions: Which one plays on interest (reward, contract)?
Which one affects a character personally?
Which one falls on them without them looking for it?
hooks.example:
- The council offers a reward to find the prince.
- A character's sister worked at the palace and has vanished.
- The regent's guards come to arrest the characters for no reason.
hooks.pitfall: A single hook, presented as an obligation: if it doesn't speak to the table, the adventure starts reluctantly.

pitch.title: The adventure at a glance
pitch.purpose: Make people want to play in a few lines: the starting situation, what the characters will do and the mood. It's the text a GM reads before picking your module.
questions: What situation troubles the characters at the start?
What will they actually have to do: investigate, explore, protect, flee?
Which image or detail sets this adventure apart?
pitch.example: A tower thought long dead lights up again above Coldvale, in the middle of the autumn fair. The characters have three days to find out who is reviving its seals before the town falls into panic.
pitch.pitfall: Giving away the ending or the central secret. The pitch is a promise of play; the hidden truth belongs in the GM-only background.

contentWarnings.title: Content warnings
contentWarnings.purpose: Warn the GM about difficult themes so they can talk about them with their table before playing, and adjust what needs adjusting.
questions: Which themes might make players uncomfortable: graphic violence, death of a child, grief, possession, harassment…?
Can a scene be played off-screen without breaking the adventure? Say so.
contentWarnings.example: Physical violence, death of a secondary character, possession. The crypt scene can be summarised rather than described.
contentWarnings.pitfall: Leaving it empty for fear of spoiling the surprise. Naming a theme reveals nothing of the plot, and a prepared GM runs it better.

gmBackground.title: Hidden background
gmBackground.purpose: What the GM needs to know and the players don't: what really happened, who wants what, and what happens if nobody steps in.
questions: What happened before the characters arrived?
Who is pulling the strings, what do they want and through which steps?
What becomes of the situation if the characters do nothing?
Can the players piece this truth together from the adventure's clues?
gmBackground.example: The tower's master isn't dead: he traded his name for his survival. His scribe revives one seal each night; at the third, he takes form again. Without the characters, the fair ends with the lower town in flames.
gmBackground.pitfall: A secret story too complicated to be discovered in play. If the players can't understand it by the end, simplify it.

hooks.title: Hooks
hooks.purpose: The reasons that bring the characters into the adventure. A published module doesn't know the buyer's characters: offer several, of different kinds.
questions: Which hook plays on interest (reward, contract, opportunity)?
Which one plays on a personal tie (a relative, a debt, a past)?
Which one starts from an event that falls on the characters without them seeking it?
hooks.example:
- The council offers 500 coins to escort a pedlar.
- A childhood friend of one character vanished in Coldvale.
- One character's medallion grows warm near the tower.
hooks.pitfall: A single hook, presented as an obligation. Players get more involved when the adventure is an opportunity they choose.

credits.title: Credits
credits.purpose: Name everyone who contributed: it's expected in a released module, and it's a mark of respect.
questions: Who wrote, illustrated, mapped, edited?
Which tables playtested the adventure?
Are you using licensed artwork or rules that must be credited?
credits.example:
Writing: Camille Martin
Maps: Léo Dubois
Editing: Alex
Playtesters: the Thursday table (Inès, Yanis, Paul, Mira)
credits.pitfall: Forgetting the playtesters, or the credits required by an artwork's or a game system's licence.

role.title: Role in the story
role.purpose: Knowing what place an NPC holds tells you how much preparation they deserve: an opponent or an ally weighs on the plot, an extra only needs one detail.
questions: Does this NPC help the characters, oppose them, or hold something they need?
Do they act on their own, or are they the prize others fight over?
role.example: Borin the blacksmith is a resource: he knows who ordered the crypt keys, but will only tell someone who helps him.
role.pitfall: Allies who do everything in the players' place. An ally has limits: what they can't or won't do.

motivation.title: Motivation
motivation.purpose: What the NPC wants decides everything they do. With a clear motivation, the GM knows how they react to anything the players do.
questions: What do they want, right now?
What are they afraid to lose?
How far are they willing to go?
motivation.example: Ysolde wants the throne for herself, but fears scandal above all: she'd rather bribe than kill.
motivation.pitfall: A villain who is evil "just because": players can neither understand, manipulate nor convince them.

knowledge.title: What they know
knowledge.purpose: Listing what the NPC can reveal avoids improvising contradictory answers and ties the NPC to the adventure's clues.
questions: What useful information do they hold?
On what condition will they share it (trust, money, threat)?
What do they wrongly believe they know?
knowledge.example: He saw the notary leave the room at midnight. He'll say so in exchange for safe passage out of town.
knowledge.pitfall: An NPC who knows everything and tells the first person who asks: the investigation is solved in one conversation.

mannerism.title: Distinctive trait
mannerism.purpose: One detail to play at the table makes an NPC memorable in seconds, and helps players recognise who is speaking.
questions: What gesture or habit gives them away?
How do they speak: fast, slowly, with a pet word?
mannerism.example: Taps her ring every time she lies, and ends her sentences with "don't you agree?".
mannerism.pitfall: A long physical description nobody remembers: one strong detail beats a full portrait.
